messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] Metagenomic Data Analysis of Microbial Communities (MGMC01) – Applications for Ecology
messages.subject_clean: Metagenomic Data Analysis of Microbial Communities (MGMC01) – Applications for Ecology
messages.body_plain:
Metagenomic Data Analysis of Microbial Communities (MGMC01) ? Applications for Ecology

26?30 October 2026 | 25 hours | ?400 | Live Online

https://prstats.org/course/metagenomic-data-analysis-of-microbial-communities-mgmc01/

Delivered by Dr Jeferyd Yepes, a bioinformatician and computational biologist specialising in metagenomics, microbial genomics and reproducible bioinformatics workflows. His research uses large-scale metagenomic analysis to investigate complex microbial communities and their functional potential, including reconstruction of Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs).

Learn how to analyse microbial communities using metagenomic data, from experimental design, sample collection and raw sequencing data through quality control, taxonomic profiling, diversity analysis, assembly, genome reconstruction and functional interpretation.

For ecologists, metagenomics provides powerful approaches for studying microbial diversity and community composition directly within natural environments. The course covers samples from environments including soil and water, and explicitly addresses the biological and ecological rationale for studying microbial communities in situ. Both targeted marker-gene approaches such as 16S/ITS and whole-genome shotgun metagenomics are covered.

What you'll gain

  *   Understand the core concepts and ecological applications of metagenomics
  *   Design robust metagenomic studies with appropriate replication and controls
  *   Understand how sample collection, storage and DNA/RNA extraction affect downstream results
  *   Compare 16S/ITS marker-gene and shotgun metagenomic approaches
  *   Understand short- and long-read sequencing strategies
  *   Perform quality control and preprocessing of raw sequencing data
  *   Remove adapters, low-quality reads and contaminants
  *   Work with OTUs and ASVs
  *   Perform taxonomic classification and microbial community profiling
  *   Calculate and interpret alpha and beta diversity
  *   Compare microbial communities among environmental conditions
  *   Perform differential abundance analyses
  *   Understand metagenomic assembly and binning
  *   Reconstruct Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs)
  *   Assess MAG completeness and contamination
  *   Perform genome annotation and taxonomic classification
  *   Explore functional and pathway-level information
  *   Apply appropriate statistical and visualisation approaches to microbial-community data
  *
Apply FAIR and reproducible-data principles to metagenomic research

Course format

  *   Dates: 26?30 October 2026
  *   Duration: 5 days, 5 hours per day (25 hours total)
  *   Format: Live online
  *   Combination of lectures and practical computational analysis
  *   Targeted and shotgun metagenomics covered
  *   Practical work includes microbial-community analysis and MAG reconstruction
  *   Course materials, code and datasets provided
  *   All sessions recorded
  *   30 days' access to recordings
  *   30 days of post-course email support
  *
Course fee: ?400

Who is this course for?

This ecology-focused version is particularly relevant to students and researchers working in:

  *   Microbial ecology
  *   Community ecology
  *   Soil ecology
  *   Aquatic and freshwater ecology
  *   Marine and coastal ecology
  *   Environmental microbiology
  *   Biodiversity research
  *   Ecosystem ecology
  *   Plant?microbe interactions
  *   Environmental change
  *   Agricultural ecology
  *   Molecular ecology
  *   Environmental genomics
  *   Microbiome research
  *   Conservation and environmental monitoring

The course is particularly useful for researchers who want to investigate microbial community composition, diversity and functional potential across species, habitats, environmental gradients or experimental conditions.

Participants should have basic familiarity with R/RStudio and data manipulation. Familiarity with UNIX/Linux is also useful for the computational components of the course.

Why take this course?

Microorganisms are fundamental components of ecological communities and play critical roles in processes ranging from decomposition and nutrient cycling to host interactions and ecosystem functioning. However, a substantial proportion of microbial diversity cannot readily be studied using traditional culture-based approaches.

Metagenomics allows microbial communities to be studied directly from environmental samples, providing information about both their taxonomic composition and functional potential. This makes metagenomic approaches particularly valuable for ecologists investigating how microbial communities vary among habitats, environmental conditions and experimental treatments.

The course takes participants through the complete analytical workflow. Marker-gene approaches provide methods for examining community composition, diversity and differences among conditions, while shotgun sequencing, assembly and MAG reconstruction allow researchers to recover and characterise individual microbial genomes and investigate their functional capabilities.

For ecologists increasingly incorporating molecular data into their research, MGMC01 provides a practical bridge between ecological questions and modern microbial-community genomics, with an emphasis on robust experimental design, reproducible analysis and biologically meaningful interpretation.

Please feel free to share this course with colleagues, friends, research groups, labs, and others within your institute, organisation, or wider research network.

Learn more & enrol

Metagenomic Data Analysis of Microbial Communities (MGMC01)

https://prstats.org/course/metagenomic-data-analysis-of-microbial-communities-mgmc01/

Questions?

Email: oliver at prstats.org<mailto:oliver at prstats.org>

Best wishes,

Oliver Hooker
PR Stats

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

Transmitting Science is offering a new edition of the live online course 
"Model-Based Statistical Inference in Evolutionary Biogeography".

Course webpage:

https://www.transmittingscience.com/courses/evolution/model-based-statistical-inference-evolutionary-biogeography-2/ 
[1]

Course overview:

This course offers a structured, hands-on introduction to methods for 
inferring historical biogeography using phylogenetic and spatial data.

Participants will learn how to estimate ancestral geographic ranges, 
compare probabilistic models, and interpret biogeographic patterns using 
real data.

The course moves from introductory training in R, phylogenies, and 
BioGeoBEARS, through likelihood-based model testing and visualisation, 
to advanced topics such as trait-dependent dispersal, state-dependent 
diversification models, and large-scale analyses. It also incorporates 
the integration of GIS and paleogeographic data (e.g., via GPlates), 
equipping participants with a comprehensive toolkit for studying 
lineages across space and time.

For any questions, please write to courses at transmittingscience.com

Best regards,

Haris

messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] Multivariate Analysis of Ecological Communities Using VEGAN (VGNR10) – Applications for Ecology
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate Analysis of Ecological Communities Using VEGAN (VGNR10) – Applications for Ecology
messages.body_plain:
Multivariate Analysis of Ecological Communities Using VEGAN (VGNR10) ? Applications for Ecology

2?6 November 2026 | 35 hours | ?485 | Live Online

https://prstats.org/course/multivariate-analysis-of-ecological-communities-using-vegan-vgnr10/

Learn how to analyse complex ecological community datasets using R and the VEGAN package, with practical training in multivariate statistical methods, ordination, clustering, community diversity and the relationships between species assemblages and environmental conditions.

This comprehensive five-day course combines statistical theory with hands-on analysis of real ecological datasets, providing researchers with the skills needed to investigate community composition, biodiversity patterns, species assemblages and ecological responses to environmental and anthropogenic gradients.

The course uses empirical datasets from terrestrial ecology, wetland ecology, microbial ecology, natural resource management, evolution and palaeoecology. Participants are strongly encouraged to bring their own datasets and will receive guidance on selecting appropriate analytical approaches, interpreting results and presenting their findings.

What you'll gain

  *   Understand the principles of multivariate analysis of ecological communities

  *   Prepare, structure and transform ecological community datasets in R

  *   Calculate and interpret diversity indices and community metrics

  *   Understand different ecological distance and dissimilarity measures

  *   Select appropriate transformations and distance measures for community data

  *   Apply clustering and classification techniques to identify patterns in species assemblages

  *   Understand and perform unconstrained ordination analyses

  *   Apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

  *   Use Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS) to visualise ecological community patterns

  *   Understand and apply constrained ordination methods

  *   Perform Redundancy Analysis (RDA)

  *   Apply Canonical Correspondence Analysis (CCA)

  *   Investigate relationships between community composition and environmental predictors

  *   Test ecological hypotheses using canonical ordination methods

  *   Analyse community responses to environmental and anthropogenic gradients

  *   Work with continuous and categorical explanatory variables

  *   Interpret and visualise multivariate results

  *   Develop reproducible analytical workflows using R and VEGAN

  *   Apply multivariate methods to your own ecological research questions and datasets

Course format

  *   Dates: 2?6 November 2026

  *   Duration: 5 days, 7 hours per day ? 35 hours total

  *   Format: Live online

  *   Combination of theoretical lectures and hands-on practical exercises

  *   Practical analysis using R and the VEGAN package

  *   Empirical datasets covering a range of ecological disciplines

  *   Participants are encouraged to bring their own datasets

  *   Individual guidance on choosing appropriate methods and interpreting results

  *   All sessions recorded, with recordings normally available the same day

  *   30 days' access to recordings

  *   Course fee: ?485

Who is this course for?

This course will be particularly relevant to researchers and postgraduate students working in:

  *   Community ecology

  *   Biodiversity research

  *   Conservation biology

  *   Terrestrial ecology

  *   Freshwater and aquatic ecology

  *   Marine and coastal ecology

  *   Wetland ecology

  *   Microbial ecology

  *   Plant ecology

  *   Forest ecology

  *   Environmental monitoring

  *   Restoration ecology

  *   Landscape ecology

  *   Palaeoecology

  *   Evolutionary ecology

  *   Natural resource management

  *   Quantitative ecology

It is particularly valuable for researchers working with species abundance, occurrence, community composition or other multivariate ecological datasets, especially where the objective is to identify community patterns, compare assemblages or investigate relationships with environmental variables.

The course is designed for participants with an intermediate understanding of R, including familiarity with basic data manipulation and statistical analysis.

Why take this course?

Ecological communities consist of multiple species whose distributions, abundances and interactions vary across habitats, environmental conditions and spatial or temporal gradients. Understanding these patterns requires statistical approaches capable of analysing multiple species and ecological variables simultaneously.

Traditional univariate analyses are often insufficient for investigating complex community-level patterns. Multivariate methods provide powerful tools for identifying differences in species assemblages, quantifying community diversity, exploring ecological gradients and evaluating relationships between community composition and environmental drivers.

The VEGAN package in R is one of the most widely used tools for multivariate community ecology, offering a comprehensive range of methods for ecological distance calculations, diversity analysis, clustering, ordination and hypothesis testing.

VGNR10 provides practical training in these methods, including PCA, NMDS, RDA and CCA, with an emphasis on understanding when each approach is appropriate, how to interpret the results and how to avoid common analytical pitfalls.

A particular strength of this course is its emphasis on applying the methods to participants' own research. Attendees are encouraged to bring their datasets and can receive guidance on refining research questions, preparing data, selecting appropriate transformations and analyses, and interpreting and presenting their results.

By the end of the course, participants will have developed the skills needed to move from raw ecological community data to robust multivariate analysis, meaningful ecological interpretation and reproducible scientific reporting.

Please feel free to share this course with colleagues, friends, research groups, labs, and others within your institute, organisation, or wider research network.

Learn more & enrol

Last June we launched the /Journal of Statistical Ecology/. Some of you 
might have heard of it already through social media or word of mouth. 
Its goals are to provide an academic journal at the interface between 
ecology and statistics, and to promote an ethical and inclusive open 
access publishing model (diamond open access: no article processing 
charges, sponsored by academic institutions). The journal website can be 
found here https://jse.centre-mersenne.org/

On the website you will find more details about the journal scope and 
its publishing model <https://jse.centre-mersenne.org/page/about/>, its

guidelines <https://jse.centre-mersenne.org/page/author-guidelines/>, 
and a link to the submission website. The journal is open to submissions 
and you are, of course, welcome to submit your recent statistical 
ecology research. Do not hesitate to send an informal inquiry if need 
be. Those are the early days of JSE and we also welcome feedback from 
the community on technical as well as thematic aspects.

messages.body_plain:
Hello R-SIG-ECOLOGY members

A reminder - Ecological datasets require thoughtful choices about display, comparison, and modelling. Statistical Foundations of Data Science with R is a 2-day seminar livestreaming October 19 and 23 with Centre for Applied Statistics Courses (CASC) (University College London). R-based data visualisation, statistical inference, and regression support analysis of ecological and environmental observations. messages.subject_clean: Online course: Spatial and Spatio-Temporal GLMs and GAMs using inlabru – November 2026
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We are organising a 5-day online course on GLMs and GAMs with spatial 
and spatio-temporal correlation using the R package inlabru, from 9?13 
November 2026.

Many data sets contain observations that are related in space or time. 
For example, observations collected close together may be more similar 
than observations collected far apart. Ignoring this dependence can 
affect the results of a statistical analysis.

In this course, we will show how to include spatial and spatio-temporal 
correlation in GLMs and GAMs using INLA and the R package inlabru.

We will work through a series of practical exercises, covering:

  *

    Adding spatial correlation to regression models.

  *

    Fitting GLMs and GAMs with spatial correlation.

  *

    Working with continuous, count and presence/absence data.

  *

    Modelling spatial correlation when there are natural barriers, such
    as coastlines.

  *

    Adding spatio-temporal correlation to GLMs and GAMs.

The course is applied and non-technical, with an emphasis on 
understanding the methods and implementing them in R. All exercises come 
with data sets and annotated R scripts.

Course details:

  *

    Dates: 9?13 November 2026

  *

    Time: 09:00?16:00 CET

  *

    Format: Live online course

  *

    Fee: ?500 (VAT where applicable)

  *

    Instructors: Dr Elena Ieno and Dr Alain Zuur

Participants will have access to the course materials and various videos 
for 12 months. The course fee also includes a one-hour individual online 
meeting with an instructor to discuss your own data or statistical 
questions related to the course.

Some experience with R, linear regression and GLMs is required. 
Preparatory materials are available for those who would like to refresh 
their knowledge before the course.

Further information and registration:

https://www.highstat.com/index.php/joine-an-onsite-course 
<https://www.highstat.com/index.php/joine-an-onsite-course>

Please feel free to forward this email to colleagues who may be interested.

Kind regards,

Alain Zuur

Highland Statistics Ltd
www.highstat.com <http://www.highstat.com/>

messages.subject_clean: JOINT SPECIES DISTRIBUTION MODELLING (JSDM) USING HMSC: A HIERARCHICAL MODELLING APPROACH IN R (JSDM01) 2 places left
messages.body_plain:
JOINT SPECIES DISTRIBUTION MODELLING (JSDM) USING HMSC: A HIERARCHICAL MODELLING APPROACH IN R (JSDM01)

Only 2 places left!

26?29 October 2026 | Live Online | 22 Hours | ?450

Instructor: Dr Bastien Parisy, University of Helsinki, Finland

Understanding how ecological communities respond to environmental change requires moving beyond modelling individual species in isolation. Joint Species Distribution Models (JSDMs) provide a powerful framework for examining entire communities, identifying environmental drivers of species distributions, and investigating patterns of species co-occurrence and community assembly.

This four-day, hands-on course introduces Hierarchical Modelling of Species Communities (HMSC), a flexible Bayesian framework for analysing multi-species ecological data in R.

Using real ecological datasets, participants will learn to:

  *   Build and fit hierarchical joint species distribution models in R.

  *   Investigate how environmental gradients influence species occurrences and abundances.

  *   Incorporate species traits, phylogenetic relationships, and spatial or temporal structure.

  *   Examine species co-occurrence, residual associations, and community assembly patterns.

  *   Assess model convergence, fit, and predictive performance.

  *   Interpret and visualise model outputs at both species and community levels.

  *   Apply HMSC to ecological research questions and report findings for scientific publication.

Who should attend?

The course is particularly relevant to community ecologists, biodiversity researchers, conservation scientists, spatial ecologists, and researchers working with multi-species datasets. It is also suitable for PhD students, postdoctoral researchers, and ecologists wishing to progress from traditional species distribution modelling to community-level approaches.

Course format: Four days of interactive lectures and practical exercises using R, with opportunities to discuss participants' own ecological datasets. All sessions are recorded, with 30 days of access following the course.

Full course details and registration:
https://prstats.org/course/joint-species-distribution-modelling-jsdm01/

Please feel free to share this course with colleagues, students, research groups, departments, and wider ecological and conservation research networks who may find it useful.
